Insolence is bold, shameless disrespect shown toward someone — especially someone who holds authority over you, or someone who deserves your respect. It's not just being rude. It's being rude without any shame, guilt, or hesitation — often with an air of arrogance, as if the person doing it feels they are above the rules, or simply does not care about the consequences.

Think of it this way: if someone is rude accidentally or out of ignorance, that's not insolence. Insolence is deliberate and brazen. The person knows they are crossing a line — and they cross it anyway, often with their head held high.
Breaking It Down Further

There are three key ingredients that make something insolence:

1. Disrespect — The behavior is dismissive, insulting, or degrading toward another person.

2. Boldness — It is done openly and without shame. The person makes no effort to hide it or soften it.

3. An imbalance in status or authority — Insolence is most commonly directed upward — from someone of lower rank toward someone of higher rank. A student toward a teacher. An employee toward a manager. A soldier toward an officer. A child toward a parent. This is a key detail: if two equals are rude to each other, you might call it rudeness or disrespect. But when someone of lower status acts with arrogant disrespect toward someone above them, that is classic insolence.
What Does It Look Like?

Insolence can show up in words, tone, or actions.

  • A student who rolls their eyes, talks back, and flatly refuses to follow the teacher's instructions — with no remorse — is showing insolence.
  • An employee who dismisses their boss's directions with a sarcastic laugh and walks away is being insolent.
  • A child who tells a parent "you can't tell me what to do" in a defiant, sneering tone is showing insolence.
  • A soldier who responds to an officer's order with a mocking smirk and a dismissive shrug is being insolent.

Notice that in each case, the person isn't just being rude — they're defying authority or dignity with confidence and without apology.
The Feeling Behind It

At the heart of insolence is a kind of arrogant contempt — a feeling that the other person is not worth your respect, or that you are above having to show them any. It can come from a place of pride, rebellion, or simply a complete lack of regard for social rules and authority.

This is what separates insolence from ordinary rudeness. Ordinary rudeness might come from a bad mood, poor manners, or carelessness. Insolence, however, carries an attitude — almost a statement: "I do not respect you, and I am not afraid to show it."
How It's Used in Sentences

• "The young soldier was punished for his insolence toward the commanding officer."
  • "She stared at her boss with open insolence, making it clear she had no intention of following the new rules."
  • "The teacher was shocked by the insolence of the student, who simply laughed when asked to sit down."
  • "Such insolence will not be tolerated in this classroom."
  • "He answered every question with an insolence that made everyone uncomfortable."
Related Word Forms

The same root gives you three other useful words:

  • Insolent (adjective) — describes a person or behavior: "an insolent reply," "an insolent child."
  • Insolently (adverb) — describes how something is done: "He insolently dismissed the officer's command."
  • Insolence (noun, which you're learning) — the quality or act itself: "Her insolence was breathtaking."
Words Close in Meaning

These words are near-siblings of insolence, but each has a slightly different shade:

  • Impudence — Very similar to insolence, but often used for behavior that is bold and cheeky in a way that can feel slightly less aggressive — like a clever child talking back. Insolence feels heavier and more confrontational.
  • Impertinence — Overstepping your boundaries; saying or doing something that is not your place. Slightly more polite-sounding than insolence.
  • Effrontery — Extreme, shocking boldness or nerve, often used when someone does something they have absolutely no right to do, with total confidence. Very close to insolence.
  • Audacity — Daring, reckless boldness. Can sometimes be used positively (brave audacity), but when used negatively, it overlaps with insolence.
  • Disrespect — The broadest, most everyday word. Insolence is a specific, proud, and bold type of disrespect.
What Insolence Is NOT

It helps to know what insolence is not, to sharpen your understanding:

  • Disagreement is not insolence. You can respectfully disagree with a boss or teacher — that's healthy. Insolence is when the disagreement is delivered with contempt, arrogance, or defiance.
  • Confidence is not insolence. Standing up for yourself calmly and firmly is not insolence. Insolence is specifically about disrespect and arrogance, not confidence.
  • Casual language is not insolence. Being informal with someone in authority isn't automatically insolent — it depends on context and tone.
The Tone of the Word

"Insolence" is a fairly formal word. You are more likely to see it in books, formal writing, professional settings, or historical and literary contexts than in everyday casual conversation. In casual speech, someone might just say "disrespect," "attitude," or "cheek." But when a writer or speaker uses the word insolence, they are signaling that the behavior was not just rude — it was jarringly, unashamedly, and boldly disrespectful.
One-Line Summary to Remember It By
Insolence is bold, shameless, arrogant disrespect — especially toward authority — delivered without guilt and without apology.
IN-suh-luhns
